'''Lazio''': {{legend0|#ffb2b2|40–50%}} {{legend0|#e27f7f|50–60%}} {{legend0|#d75d5d|60–70%}} | title = U.S. Senator | before_election = [[Daniel Patrick Moynihan]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Hillary Rodham Clinton]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) }}{{ElectionsNY}} In the [[United States Senate]] election held in the [[New York (state)|State of New York]] on November 7, 2000, [[Hillary Clinton|Hillary Rodham Clinton]], then [[first lady of the United States]] and the first presidential spouse to run for political office, defeated [[United States House of Representatives|U.S. representative]] [[Rick Lazio]]. The general election coincided with the [[2000 United States presidential election|U.S. presidential election]]. The race began in November 1998 when four-term incumbent senator [[Daniel Patrick Moynihan]] announced his retirement, making this the first open Senate seat in New York since the [[1958 United States Senate election in New York|1958 Senate election]]. Both the [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic Party]] and [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican Party]] sought high-profile candidates to compete for the open seat. By early 1999, Clinton and [[Mayor of New York City|New York City mayor]] [[Rudy Giuliani]] were the frontrunners for their parties' respective nominations. Clinton and her husband, President [[Bill Clinton]], purchased a house in [[Chappaqua, New York]], in September 1999; she thereby became eligible for the election, although she faced accusations of [[Carpetbagger|carpetbagging]] since she had never resided in the state before. The lead in statewide polls swung from Clinton to Giuliani and back to Clinton as the campaigns featured both successful strategies and mistakes as well as dealing with current events. In late April and May 2000, Giuliani's medical, romantic, marital, and political lives all collided in a tumultuous four-week period, culminating in his withdrawal from the race on May 19. The Republicans chose lesser-known U.S. representative Rick Lazio to replace him. The election included a record $90 million in campaign expenditures between Clinton, Lazio, and Giuliani and national visibility. Clinton showed strength in normally Republican upstate areas and a debate blunder by Lazio solidified Clinton's previously shaky support among women. Clinton won the election in November 2000 with 55 percent of the vote to Lazio's 43 percent, and became the first woman elected to the Senate from New York. == Background == When four-term senator [[Daniel Patrick Moynihan]] announced his retirement in November 1998,{{cite news | url=http://www.cnn.com/ALLPOLITICS/stories/1998/11/06/moynihan/ | title=Moynihan tells friends he won't seek another term | author=John King | publisher=[[CNN]]| date=November 6, 1998 | access-date=November 1, 2007 | author-link=John King (journalist)}} his previously safe U.S. Senate seat became open in the [[2000 United States Senate elections|2000 U.S. Senate elections]]. Both parties tried to find high-profile candidates to run for it. [[File:Nita Lowey.jpg|thumb|left|U.S. representative [[Nita Lowey]] was initially expected to run, but she stepped aside in favor of First Lady [[Hillary Rodham Clinton]].]] [[Mayor of New York City|New York City mayor]] [[Rudy Giuliani]], who was prevented by term limits from running for mayoral reelection in 2001, immediately indicated interest. Due to his high profile and visibility, Giuliani was supported by the New York State Republican Party, even though he had irritated many by endorsing incumbent Democratic governor [[Mario Cuomo]] over Republican [[George Pataki]] in 1994.{{cite news | title=1994 Ad | url=http://www.findarticles.com/p/articles/mi_m1282/is_n22_v46/ai_15999869 | magazine=[[National Review]] | date=November 21, 1994 | access-date=November 2, 2007 | url-status=usurped | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071201024401/http://findarticles.com/p/articles/mi_m1282/is_n22_v46/ai_15999869 | issue=22 | volume=46 | archive-date=December 1, 2007 }} Giuliani became the presumptive Republican nominee, and by April 1999 had formed a formal exploratory committee for a Senate run. There were still possible Republican primary opponents. [[Rick Lazio]], a [[United States House of Representatives|U.S. representative]] representing [[Suffolk County, New York|Suffolk County]] on [[Long Island]], was raising money and had a candidacy announcement scheduled for August 16;{{cite news | url=http://www.cnn.com/ALLPOLITICS/stories/1999/08/11/senate.2000/lazio.suspends/index.html | title=Lazio suspends Senate plans | publisher=[[CNN]] | date=August 11, 1999 | access-date=November 2, 2007 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20060825204303/http://www.cnn.com/ALLPOLITICS/stories/1999/08/11/senate.2000/lazio.suspends/index.html |archive-date = August 25, 2006}} he had openly discussed a primary against Giuliani, believing his more conservative record would be appealing to Republican primary voters. In early August, under pressure from state and national Republican figures, Pataki endorsed Giuliani. Pataki prevailed upon Lazio to forgo his candidacy, which Lazio agreed to despite frustration that Giuliani had still not officially announced that he was running; Lazio said, "If the mayor wants to be a candidate, I think he needs to get into this race. It is time to put the soap opera aside and step up to the plate." [[Nassau County, New York|Nassau County]] U.S. representative [[Peter King (American politician)|Peter T. King]] also considered running and had raised some funds. U.S. representative [[Nita Lowey]] was the candidate first expected to be the Democratic nominee,{{cite news | url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-srv/politics/campaigns/keyraces2000/stories/lowey030299.htm | title=Rep. Nita Lowey's Senate Bid on Standby | author=Kevin Merida | newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] | date=March 2, 1999 | access-date=November 1, 2007}} while other mentioned possible candidates included [[secretary of housing and urban development]] [[Andrew Cuomo]], [[New York State Comptroller|state comptroller]] [[Carl McCall]], as well as U.S. representative [[Carolyn Maloney]].{{cite news |author=Tracey Tully |date=December 31, 1998 |title=Cuomo Pushed for Senate |url=https://www.nydailynews.com/1998/12/31/cuomo-pushed-for-senate/ |access-date=26 September 2024 |newspaper=[[Daily News (New York)|Daily News]] |location=New York}} State Democratic figures were concerned that neither Lowey nor the others had the star power to rival Giuliani, and that the seat would be lost.{{citation needed|date=May 2026}} Late in 1998, prominent Democratic politicians and advisors, including U.S. representative [[Charles Rangel]],{{cite web | url=http://www.house.gov/apps/list/hearing/ny15_rangel/opedclintonharlem.html | title=Clinton Is Welcome in Harlem | author=[[Charles Rangel]] | publisher=[[United States House of Representatives]] | date=February 14, 2001 | access-date=November 2, 2007 | url-status=dead | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070329171834/http://www.house.gov/apps/list/hearing/ny15_rangel/opedclintonharlem.html | archive-date=March 29, 2007 }} urged First Lady [[Hillary Rodham Clinton]] to run for the U.S. Senate seat. An unprecedented action if she did it, Clinton spent considerable time mulling over the idea while Lowey waited in the wings. Her political advisors told her the race would be difficult and some of them told her she would lose. She waited for the [[Impeachment of Bill Clinton|impeachment proceedings of Bill Clinton]] to conclude,{{cite book | last=Gerth | first=Jeff | author-link=Jeff Gerth | author2=[[Don Van Natta, Jr.]] | title=Her Way: The Hopes and Ambitions of Hillary Rodham Clinton | year=2007 | publisher=[[Little, Brown and Company]] | location=New York | isbn=978-0-316-01742-8 | url=https://archive.org/details/herwayhopesambit00gert }}, pp. 203–204. which they did with his acquittal on February 12, 1999. ==Initial campaigns== === Early Clinton campaign === On February 16, 1999, the First Lady's office announced that she was considering running for the Senate seat. Once it was clear Clinton was going to run, Lowey stepped aside, although she would be disappointed at the lost opportunity.{{cite news | url=http://marcambinder.theatlantic.com/archives/2008/11/clinton_move_starts_more_senat.php | title=Clinton move starts more Senate jockeying | author=Ambinder, Marc | magazine=[[The Atlantic]] | date=November 21, 2008 | access-date=December 1, 2008 | author-link=Marc Ambinder | url-status=dead | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081218063840/http://marcambinder.theatlantic.com/archives/2008/11/clinton_move_starts_more_senat.php | archive-date=December 18, 2008 }} Clinton’s political adviser, [[Harold M. Ickes|Harold Ickes]], lead the campaign during its early stages. Ickes assembled the initial campaign team, which included [[Terry McAuliffe]] and Laura Hartigan. Both had previously been the most senior members of Bill Clinton's finance team during his [[Bill Clinton 1996 presidential campaign|1996 reelection campaign]].{{Cite web |date=1999-06-14 |title=Hillary Banks Senate Donations - CBS News |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/hillary-banks-senate-donations/ |access-date=2025-04-05 |website=www.cbsnews.com |language=en-US}}{{Cite news |last=Glasser |first=Susan B. |date=1999-06-15 |title=First Lady Prepares to Raise Funds |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/politics/1999/06/15/first-lady-prepares-to-raise-funds/33db179e-4902-4fe4-baf7-b708ae20db05/ |access-date=2026-09-14 |work=The Washington Post |language=en-US |issn=0190-8286}} In December 1999, after a series of campaign missteps, [[Bill de Blasio]] was brought on as the full-time campaign manager.{{Cite news |last=Nagourney |first=Adam |date=1999-12-04 |title=Clinton Senate Campaign Gets a Full-Time Director |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1999/12/04/nyregion/clinton-senate-campaign-gets-a-full-time-director.html |access-date=2026-09-14 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}} On July 7, 1999, Clinton formally announced an exploratory committee for the Senate run;Gerth, Van Natta Jr., ''Her Way'', pp. 208–209. the setting was Moynihan's farm in Pindars Corners, in rural [[Delaware County, New York|Delaware County]].{{cite book | last=Bernstein | first=Carl | author-link=Carl Bernstein | title=A Woman in Charge: The Life of Hillary Rodham Clinton | url=https://archive.org/details/womaninchargel00bern | url-access=registration | year=2007 | publisher=Alfred A. Knopf | location=New York | isbn=978-0-375-40766-6 }}, p. 540. Bill Clinton was less than enthusiastic about her candidacy. The staging of the event was brokered by the Clintons' political consultant [[Mandy Grunwald]].{{cite news | url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9900E7DD1E3FF933A15754C0A96F958260 | title=Public Lives: A Top Adviser to a Much-Advised First Lady | author=[[Elisabeth Bumiller]] | newspaper=[[The New York Times]] | date=July 20, 1999 | access-date=October 24, 2007}} Hillary Clinton embarked upon a "listening tour" of all parts of New York after her entrance into the race.[[Hillary Rodham Clinton]], ''[[Living History (book)|Living History]]'', Simon & Schuster, 2003, {{ISBN|0-7432-2224-5}}, pp. 508. She planned to visit all 62 counties in New York, talking to New Yorkers in small-group settings according to the principles of [[retail politics]].Gerth, Van Natta Jr., ''Her Way'', p. 210. During the race, she spent considerable time campaigning in traditionally Republican upstate regions. Clinton faced charges of [[carpetbagging]], since she had never resided in the State of New York nor directly participated in state politics prior to her Senate race. Meanwhile, in September 1999, the Clintons purchased a $1.7 million, 11-room, [[Dutch Colonial Revival architecture|Dutch Colonial style]] home in [[Chappaqua, New York]], north of New York City.{{cite news | author=[[Adam Nagourney]] | url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9503E5D8153AF930A3575AC0A96F958260 | title=With Some Help, Clintons Purchase a White House | newspaper=The New York Times | date=September 3, 1999 | access-date=June 2, 2007}} Even the commonplace activity of house hunting leading up to this was the subject of considerable media attention; coverage of personal lives would be the norm in this contest of two "electrifying and polarizing figures" (as one reporter put it).{{cite news | author=[[Adam Nagourney]] | title= Unusual Scrutiny for a Senate Race: This Time It's Personal | url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9D00E4DE103BF93AA1575BC0A96F958260 | date=August 29, 1999 | newspaper=The New York Times | access-date=September 30, 2007}} In November 1999, Hillary Clinton announced that she would set aside most of her official duties as First Lady in order to take up residency in New York and pursue her campaign.{{cite news | url=https://www.nytimes.com/1999/11/24/nyregion/mrs-clinton-to-be-official-new-yorker.html | title=Mrs. Clinton to Be Official New Yorker | author=John M. Broder | newspaper=The New York Times | date=November 24, 1999 | access-date=April 23, 2015}} Her move-in took place in January 2000, with the house furnished with many of the couple's possessions from their Arkansas days.{{cite news | url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-srv/WPcap/2000-01/05/073r-010500-idx.html | title=Hillary Clinton Makes a Historic Move | author=Lynne Duke | newspaper=The Washington Post | date=January 5, 2000 | access-date=April 23, 2015}} It became the first time since [[Woodrow Wilson]]'s first wife died in 1914 that a president lived in the White House without a spouse. The early stages of her campaign were not without mistakes, and as she later wrote, "Mistakes in New York politics aren't easily brushed aside."''Living History'', p. 509. In a much-publicized move, Clinton donned a [[New York Yankees]] baseball cap at a June 1999 event when she had been a lifelong fan of the [[Chicago Cubs]].{{cite news | url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9F07E1DD1738F932A25755C0A96F958260 | title= Mrs. Clinton May Steal Mayor's Yankee Fan Base | author=Katherine Q. Seelye | newspaper=The New York Times | date=June 11, 1999 | access-date=February 20, 2008}}{{cite news | url=http://www.time.com/time/pacific/magazine/20001120/first_lady.html | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20010305114203/http://www.time.com/time/pacific/magazine/20001120/first_lady.html | url-status=dead | archive-date=March 5, 2001 | title=Capitol Hill | author=[[Margaret Carlson]] | magazine=[[Time (magazine)|Time]] | date=November 20, 2000 | access-date=December 8, 2007}}{{cite news | url=http://www.businessweek.com/bwdaily/dnflash/oct2000/nf20001025_071.htm | title=The Subway Series, Hillary, and Rick | author=Ciro Scotti | magazine=[[Bloomberg BusinessWeek]] | date=October 25, 2000 | access-date=December 8, 2007 | url-status=dead | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060613200341/http://www.businessweek.com/bwdaily/dnflash/oct2000/nf20001025_071.htm | archive-date=June 13, 2006 }} This brought her much criticism, and Thomas Kuiper would later write an anti-Clinton book titled: ''I've Always Been a Yankees Fan: Hillary Clinton in Her Own Words''. Clinton said she had to develop an [[American League]] rooting interest, since fans of the Cubs were not expected to root for the American League [[Chicago White Sox]].{{cite news | url=https://nymag.com/nymetro/news/sports/features/3943/ | title=Baseball Ballot | author=Chris Smith & Jessica Lustig | magazine=[[New York (magazine)|New York]] | date=October 16, 2000 | access-date=December 8, 2007}} In her 2003 autobiography, she said that putting on the hat had been a "bad move", but reiterated what had been reported in the press prior to the incident, that she had been "a die-hard [[Mickey Mantle]] fan;"''Living History'', p 509. the book included a photograph of her with a Yankees cap on from 1992.''Living History'', plate 40, first photo section. More seriously, on November 11, 1999, at the dedication of a U.S.-funded health program in the [[West Bank]], she exchanged kisses with [[Suha Arafat]], wife of Palestinian president [[Yasser Arafat]], after Suha Arafat had delivered a speech claiming that [[Israel]] had deliberately poisoned Palestinians through environmental degradation and the use of "poisonous gas".{{cite news | url=http://edition.cnn.com/WORLD/meast/9911/12/mideast.hillary.02/ | title=Diplomatic flap follows Hillary Clinton to Jordan | publisher=[[CNN]]| date=November 12, 1999 | access-date=February 3, 2016 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20050419180807/http://www.cnn.com/WORLD/meast/9911/11/israel.hillary.02/ |archive-date = April 19, 2005}} Some Israeli supporters said that Clinton never should have kissed the wife of the Palestinian leader, especially after such inflammatory remarks. The following day, Clinton denounced Suha Arafat's allegations, and said that Palestinian negotiator [[Saeb Erekat]] had told her Suha Arafat had been referring to '[[tear gas]]' and not '[[poison gas]]'. The kiss became a campaign issue, especially with Jewish voters.{{cite news | url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9F00E3D9153DF937A25752C1A96F958260 | title= Hillary Clinton Strikes Back At Giuliani on Mideast Trip | author=Joel Greenberg | newspaper=The New York Times | date=November 14, 1999 | access-date=February 20, 2008}} Clinton said it was a formality akin to a handshake, saying that to not have done so would have caused a diplomatic incident.{{cite news | url=http://archives.cnn.com/2000/ALLPOLITICS/stories/09/11/lazio.arafat.ap/ | title=Hillary Clinton's rival defends handshake with Arafat | author=Beth J. Harpaz | agency=[[Associated Press]] | publisher=[[CNN]] | date=September 11, 2000 | access-date=December 8, 2007 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20070601031653/http://archives.cnn.com/2000/ALLPOLITICS/stories/09/11/lazio.arafat.ap/ |archive-date = June 1, 2007}} Clinton later wrote that the live [[Arabic language|Arabic]]-to-English translation had failed to convey the accurate nature of her remarks: "Had I been aware of her hateful words, I would have denounced them on the spot."''Living History'', pp. 509–510. Clinton faced an erosion of support from women voters during her campaign, with her numbers declining throughout 1999.{{cite news | url=https://www.nytimes.com/2000/02/22/nyregion/clinton-campaign-confronts-erosion-of-women-s-support.html | title=Clinton Campaign Confronts Erosion of Women's Support | author=[[Elisabeth Bumiller]] | newspaper=The New York Times | date=February 22, 2000 | access-date=February 21, 2010}} This was partly a typical pattern seen with women candidates where they have an early surge of female support, which then wears off, and it was partly due to her early campaign stumbles. But it also reflected the particular set of mixed feelings that women had towards Clinton's marriage and the ambition and the power she derived from it. The problem was especially acute among some female demographics; one of her longtime advisers later said, "Women in the educated professional class? They fucking couldn't stand her. We could never figure out why. We had psychologists come in."{{cite book | first=Anne E. | last=Kornblut | author-link=Anne E. Kornblut | title=Notes from the Cracked Ceiling: Hillary Clinton, Sarah Palin, and What It Will Take for a Woman to Win | publisher=[[Crown Books]] | location=New York | year=2009 | isbn=978-0-307-46425-5 | page=[https://archive.org/details/notesfromcracked00korn/page/31 31] | url=https://archive.org/details/notesfromcracked00korn/page/31 }} Clinton's campaign to all counties, carried by a [[Ford Motor Company|Ford]] [[conversion van]], helped to defuse the carpetbagger issue,Bernstein, ''A Woman in Charge'', p. 542 with many New York residents saying that Clinton "seems like one of us." She discussed local issues such as [[price support]]s for the [[dairy industry]], fares for air travel, [[college tuition]] levels, and the [[brain drain]] in parts of the state.{{cite news | url=http://www.salon.com/news/feature/2007/11/27/rudy_hillary/ | title=When Rudy Met Hillary | author=Rob Polner | magazine=[[Salon (magazine)|Salon]] | date=November 27, 2007 | access-date=February 22, 2008}} Her political positions were well matched to the different constituencies in the state that she targeted. In a January 2000 appearance on the ''[[Late Show with David Letterman]]'', she established a rapport with the host that would continue throughout her Senate years and into her 2008 presidential campaign.Gerth, Van Natta Jr., ''Her Way'', p. 211. Clinton formally announced her official candidacy in [[Purchase, New York]] in February 2000, adopting the simple name "Hillary" for her campaign literature. Distrustful of the press since [[Bill Clinton presidential campaign, 1992|her husband's 1992 presidential campaign]] and her early days as First Lady,{{cite news | url=http://www.tnr.com/politics/story.html?id=6e01fdce-ad97-4dab-a07d-bf98dc52f681 | author=[[Michael Crowley (journalist)|Michael Crowley]] | title=Bunker Hillary | magazine=[[The New Republic]] | date=November 12, 2007 | access-date=December 6, 2007}} she imposed limits on her availability to the press van following her. [[Associated Press]] reporter Beth Harpaz later recounted a typical day from this time: "But we'd been told there'd be no 'avail' today, and we'd accepted it. That didn't prevent me from feeling slightly humiliated. I was so worn down and so exasperated by the lack of access and the lack of news in this campaign that I'd given up fighting."{{cite book | last=Harpaz | first=Beth | title=The Girls in the Van: Covering Hillary | publisher=[[St. Martin's Press]] | year=2001 | isbn=978-0-312-30271-9 | url=https://archive.org/details/girlsinvan00beth }} p. 86. === Early Giuliani campaign === An early January 1999 [[Marist Institute of Public Opinion]] poll showed Giuliani trailing Clinton by 10 points.{{cite news | url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9A05E3DB113CF932A05752C0A9669C8B63 | title=Losing the Women | author=Lee M. Miringoff | newspaper=The New York Times | date=January 31, 2000 | access-date=September 27, 2007}} By January 2000, the Marist poll showed Giuliani up by 9 points. Giuliani's tactics involved intentionally baiting the Clinton campaign with deliberate overstatements, keeping them off balance and behind in the response cycle.{{cite news | url=https://www.nytimes.com/2007/11/28/us/politics/28york.html | title=Senate Race That Fizzled Honed Skills for '08 | author=[[Adam Nagourney]] | newspaper=The New York Times | date=November 28, 2007 | access-date=November 29, 2007}} Giuliani emphasized his depiction of Clinton as a carpetbagger. He made a one-day visit to [[Little Rock, Arkansas]], where he announced he would fly the Arkansas state flag over New York's City Hall. When Hillary Clinton visited New York from Washington, he said, "I hope she knows the way. I hope she doesn't get lost on one of the side streets." Giuliani's campaign prepared a 315-page [[opposition research]] dossier that went back to her time at [[Wellesley College]]; it included eleven pages of what they termed "Stupid Actions and Remarks". The Giuliani campaign had no problems raising money, getting over 40 percent of its funds from out-of-state and outraising Clinton overall two-to-one. The Giuliani campaign showed some structural weaknesses. So closely identified with New York City, he had somewhat limited appeal to naturally Republican voters in [[Upstate New York]].{{cite news | url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9E06E0DD163AF935A35752C1A96F958260 | title= Looking for the Senator From All of New York | author=George Gates | newspaper=The New York Times | date=November 6, 1999 | access-date=September 27, 2007}} The [[Farmersville Garbage Scandal]] was indicative of his lower levels of support upstate.{{cite web | url=http://concernedcitizens.homestead.com/newspagenew.html | title=What's a 'Community'? | publisher=Concerned Citizens of Cattaraugus County | date=October 27, 2006 | access-date=December 8, 2007}} By late December 1999, Clinton adapted to Giuliani's [[psychological warfare]], saying in response to one such gambit, "I can't be responding every time the mayor gets angry. Because that's all I would do." A February 2000 attempt by Giuliani to capitalize on a Clinton campaign event's accidental playing of [[Billy Joel]]'s suburban drug tale "[[Captain Jack (Billy Joel song)|Captain Jack]]"{{cite news | url=http://www.vh1.com/artists/news/621078/02082000/joel_billy.jhtml | title=Billy Joel Did Start The Fire In NY Senate Campaign | author=Brian Hiatt | publisher=[[VH1]] | date=February 8, 2000 | access-date=February 22, 2008 | url-status=dead | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071001010154/http://www.vh1.com/artists/news/621078/02082000/joel_billy.jhtml | archive-date=October 1, 2007 }} led to more ridicule for him than for her. On March 11, 2000, Giuliani and Clinton met face-to-face for the first time since the campaigning began, at the New York Inner Circle press dinner, an annual event in which New York politicians and the press corps stage skits, [[roast (comedy)|roast]] each other and make fun of themselves, with proceeds going to charity.{{cite web | url=http://1010wins.com/pages/8015.php?contentType=4&contentId=102423 | title=Our Staff: Glenn Schuck | publisher=[[WINS (AM)|WINS]] | access-date=December 8, 2007 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20071104020301/http://www.1010wins.com/pages/8015.php?contentType=4&contentId=102423 |archive-date = November 4, 2007}} Giuliani was on stage in male [[disco]] garb spoofing [[John Travolta]] in ''[[Saturday Night Fever]]'', but also appeared [[drag (clothing)|in drag]] in taped video clips that reworked the "Rudy/Rudia" theme of a past Inner Circle dinner,{{cite web|url=https://www.salon.com/test/2000/03/13/trail_mix_20/|title=Rudy does 'Saturday Night Fever'|last=Garrone|first=Max|date=March 13, 2000|website=[[Salon.com|Salon]]|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200208055502/https://www.salon.com/test/2000/03/13/trail_mix_20/|archive-date=February 8, 2020}} as well as in an exchange with [[Joan Rivers]] that sought to make fun of Clinton.{{cite news | author=Beth J. Harpaz | url=http://www.hillary.org/hc/Hillary_Clinton_Forum_178_chat1.cgi | title=Spoofs Target First Lady, Giuliani | agency=[[Associated Press]] | date=March 2000 | access-date=March 12, 2007 | url-status=dead | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071007170940/http://www.hillary.org/hc/Hillary_Clinton_Forum_178_chat1.cgi | archive-date=October 7, 2007 }} Other performers' skits made fun of Clinton's Yankees claim and the infidelity of her husband. The [[New York Police Department]]'s fatal shooting of [[Patrick Dorismond]] on March 15, 2000, inflamed Giuliani's already strained relations with the city's minority communities, and Clinton seized on it as a major campaign issue. By April, reports showed Clinton gaining upstate and generally outworking Giuliani, who stated that his duties as mayor prevented him from campaigning more.{{cite news | url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=980DE4DB1E3FF93BA35757C0A9669C8B63 | title= Despite Polls, Giuliani Says That He Won't Alter His Campaign Style | author=[[Adam Nagourney]] | newspaper=The New York Times | date=April 8, 2000 | access-date=September 27, 2007}} He gave priority to city duties over campaign activities. Some Giuliani aides and national Republican figures concluded that his interest in the campaign was flagging, as although he was desirous of winning in political combat against a Clinton, he was by nature an executive personality and the prospect of serving as one of a hundred legislators was unappealing to him. By this time, Clinton was 8 to 10 points ahead of Giuliani in the polls.''Living History'', p. 515. In retrospect, ''[[The New York Times]]'' would write that the battle so far between the two had comprised "a blistering year of mental gamesmanship, piercing attacks, contrasts in personalities and positions, and blunders played out by two outsize political figures in a super-heated atmosphere." === Giuliani's tumultuous four weeks === [[File:Rudy Giuliani 2000.jpg|thumb|left|[[Rudy Giuliani]] was the presumptive Republican nominee for most of 1999 and 2000, until he abruptly withdrew on May 19, 2000, following a cancer diagnosis and the public collapse of his marriage to [[Donna Hanover]].]] Giuliani's marriage to his wife, broadcast journalist and actress [[Donna Hanover]], had been distant since 1996, and the two were rarely seen in public together.{{cite news | url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9E03E4D61E39F937A35756C0A9669C8B63 | title= Mayor Acknowledges 'Very Good Friend' | author=[[Elisabeth Bumiller]] | newspaper=The New York Times | date=May 4, 2000 | access-date=December 7, 2007}} There had been no formal announcement of any change in their relationship, although Hanover had indicated that she and their children would not move to Washington if Giuliani won the race.{{cite news | title=New York Political Corner | newspaper=[[New York Amsterdam News]] | date=March 23, 2000}} Beginning in October 1999, a new woman was being spotted at mayoral functions.{{cite book | last=Barrett | first=Wayne | author-link=Wayne Barrett | title=Rudy! An Investigative Biography of Rudolph Giuliani | publisher=[[Basic Books]] | year=2000 | isbn=978-0-7567-6114-1}} p. 434. By March 2000, Giuliani had stopped wearing his wedding ring and was being seen more in the company of this other woman, including at the Inner Circle press dinner, the [[St. Patrick's Day]] parade, and town hall meetings, but it was not yet fully clear whether the relationship was personal or professional.Harpaz, ''The Girls in the Van'', p. 113. While this woman had become a frequent subject of insider talk among the New York political circle, she had not been mentioned in the press. On April 20 Hanover announced that she would soon be taking over the lead role in [[Eve Ensler]]'s controversial play ''[[The Vagina Monologues]]''.{{cite news | url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9807E7D61E31F932A15757C0A9669C8B63 | title= 'Monologues' Making A Political Connection | first=Jesse | last=McKinley | newspaper=The New York Times | date=April 21, 2000 | access-date=December 7, 2007}} Political observers speculated that Hanover was partly engaging in a political act against her husband, as Ensler was a friend and supporter of Hillary Clinton and the role would not go over well with [[social conservative]]s within the Republican Party. Giuliani declined to say whether he would attend one of her performances.{{cite news | title=People in the News | newspaper=[[St. Louis Post-Dispatch]] | date=April 27, 2000}} On April 22, the ''[[New York Post]]'' obtained photographs of Giuliani openly strolling on a Manhattan street with the other woman after they left a restaurant, but did not have more than a first name for her;Barrett, ''Rudy!'', p. 437. the ''Post'' sat on the story, but it was clear the relationship was a personal one. On April 26, television channel [[NY1]] reported that Giuliani had undergone a second round of tests for [[prostate cancer]] at [[Mount Sinai Health System|Mount Sinai Medical Center]];{{cite news | url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9E05E5DD1E30F934A15757C0A9669C8B63 | title= Giuliani Is Tested For Prostate Cancer | newspaper=The New York Times | date=April 27, 2000 | access-date=December 7, 2007}} the same disease had led to the death of his father. On April 28, Giuliani held a news conference to announce that he did in fact have prostate cancer, but it was in an early stage.{{cite news | url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9E0CE0D61F30F93BA15757C0A9669C8B63 | title= Giuliani Fighting Prostate Cancer; Unsure on Senate | author=[[Elisabeth Bumiller]] | newspaper=The New York Times | date=April 28, 2000 | access-date=December 7, 2007}} He was unsure of which of several types of treatment he might undergo, and that decision would impact whether he could stay in the Senate race or not. Hanover was not present at the conference, but issued a note saying she would support him in his decision process.{{cite news | url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9903E3DE1639F93BA15757C0A9669C8B63 | title=A Glimpse Of Giuliani, Man of Grace | author=[[Clyde Haberman]] | newspaper=The New York Times | date=April 28, 2000 | access-date=December 17, 2007}} As Giuliani mulled over his medical options, on May 1 Hanover announced that she was postponing her appearance in ''The Vagina Monologues'' due to "personal family circumstances."{{cite news | url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9407E4DA1339F931A35756C0A9669C8B63 | title= Giuliani's Wife Postpones Her Role in 'Monologues' | author=[[Elisabeth Bumiller]] | newspaper=The New York Times | date=May 2, 2000 | access-date=December 7, 2007}} On May 2 the ''[[New York Daily News]]'' published a brief item about Giuliani's other woman, without name or description.Barrett, ''Rudy!'', p. 436. On May 3 the ''New York Post'' finally published its photographs of Giuliani and the woman, now identified as [[Judith Nathan]], leaving a restaurant together, under the front-page headline "Rudy's Mystery Brunch Pal is Upper East Side Divorcée".{{cite news | url=http://transcripts.cnn.com/TRANSCRIPTS/0005/06/rs.00.html | title=Joe Lockhart Discusses Bill Clinton's Press Coverage | work=[[Reliable Sources]] | publisher=[[CNN]] | date=May 6, 2000 | access-date=December 17, 2007 | archive-date=March 3, 2016 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303212056/http://transcripts.cnn.com/TRANSCRIPTS/0005/06/rs.00.html | url-status=dead }} (Some observers felt that Giuliani, known for his ability to manipulate the New York media,{{cite news | newspaper=The New York Times | date=May 8, 2000 | author=Joyce Purnick | url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9B01E4DF1338F93BA35756C0A9669C8B63 | title='Good Friend,' A Marriage, And Voters | access-date=April 4, 2008}} had been eager for news of the relationship to come out.) Later that day, Giuliani responded to a barrage of questions on the subject at a news conference by acknowledging Judith Nathan publicly for the first time, calling her "a very good friend" and expressing his annoyance that her privacy was being invaded. The next days were filled with New York media coverage on Nathan's background and on the relationship. On May 6 Hanover held an unusually-located news conference at the back of [[St. Patrick's Cathedral, New York|St. Patrick's Cathedral]] before the funeral of [[Cardinal John O'Connor]];{{cite news | url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9B06E3DE1238F934A35756C0A9669C8B63 | title= Hanover Says Her Marriage To Mayor Is 'Very Precious' | author=Katherine E. Finkelstein | newspaper=The New York Times | date=May 7, 2000 | access-date=December 8, 2007}} visibly trembling, she said, "I will be supportive of Rudy in his fight against his illness, as this marriage and this man have been very precious to me." The following day half the press tried to stake out Nathan's known locations while the rest pestered Nathan's hometown relatives in [[Hazleton, Pennsylvania]];Barrett, ''Rudy!'', p. 438. Giuliani looked weak in a public appearance. On May 10, Giuliani held what ''The New York Times'' described as an "extraordinary, emotional news conference" in [[Bryant Park]] to announce that he was seeking a separation from Hanover,{{cite news | url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9E04E7D8163BF932A25756C0A9669C8B63 | title=Giuliani and His Wife of 16 Years Are Separating | author=[[Elisabeth Bumiller]] | newspaper=The New York Times | date=May 11, 2000 | access-date=December 8, 2007}} saying, "This is very, very painful. For quite some time it's probably been apparent that Donna and I lead in many ways independent and separate lives." Regarding Nathan, Giuliani said "I'm going to need her now more than maybe I did before", making reference to his battle with cancer and her background in nursing. Regarding the Senate race, he again did not commit to a decision, saying, "I don't really care about politics right now. I'm thinking about my family, the people that I love and what can be done that's honest and truthful and that protects them the best. I'm not thinking about politics. Politics comes at least second, maybe third, maybe fourth, somewhere else. It'll all work itself out some way politically." Giuliani had, however, neglected to inform Hanover in advance of his announcement; her reaction was described as distraught. Three hours later, she held her own news conference at [[Gracie Mansion]], where she said, "Today's turn of events brings me great sadness. I had hoped to keep this marriage together. For several years, it was difficult to participate in Rudy's public life because of his relationship with one staff member." In this, she was making reference to [[Cristyne Lategano]], the former communications director for Giuliani; ''[[Vanity Fair (magazine)|Vanity Fair]]'' had reported in 1997 that Lategano and Giuliani were having an affair, which both of them had denied.{{cite news | url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/the-women-in-giulianis-life/ | title=The Women In Giuliani's Life | publisher=[[CBS News]] | date=May 11, 2000 | access-date=December 8, 2007}} Hanover continued, "Beginning last May, I made a major effort to bring us back together. Rudy and I re-established some of our personal intimacy through the fall. At that point, he chose another path." State Republican leaders, who until now had avoided talk of replacements for Giuliani should he not run, now gave more attention to the matter, with the state party convention coming up on May 30.{{cite news | url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9C04E5D9163BF932A25756C0A9669C8B63 | title=G.O.P. Politely Searches For an Alternative, Fast | author=[[Adam Nagourney]] | newspaper=The New York Times | date=May 11, 2000 | access-date=December 18, 2007}} Former possible contenders Rick Lazio and Pete King immediately indicated they were available;{{cite news | url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9800EEDB103BF936A25756C0A9669C8B63 | title= Behind the Scenes, Efforts to Find a Possible Senate Replacement | author=Eric Lipton | newspaper=The New York Times | date=May 15, 2000 | access-date=December 18, 2007}} other names mentioned included Wall Street financier [[Theodore J. Forstmann]] and Governor Pataki, although the latter indicated no interest. Giuliani continued to ponder his Senate race decision; when he had dinner with Nathan on May 12, they were trailed by a flock of photographers.{{cite news | url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9502EEDC133BF937A25756C0A9669C8B63 | title= Giuliani Drops Upstate Fund-Raising Trip | author=Sarah Kershaw | newspaper=The New York Times | date=May 14, 2000 | access-date=December 18, 2007}} Giuliani canceled campaigning and fundraising trips to upstate New York and California on May 13, suggesting he would not run, but then resumed fundraising and suggested he was inclined towards running on May 15.{{cite news | url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9A0CE3DF1E3BF935A25756C0A9669C8B63 | title= Mayor Inclined Toward Run, But His Backers Are Nervous | author=[[Elisabeth Bumiller]] | newspaper=The New York Times | date=May 16, 2000 | access-date=December 18, 2007}} Two Republican county chairmen became upset at the indecision, saying, "Like ''Waiting for Godot'', we have ''Waiting for Rudy''", and, "We need a decision. Like tomorrow would be nice. Because this is getting ridiculous." A top state Republican said, "He seem[s] to like the attention. He seems to be going through some sort of catharsis in public. And we're like psychiatrists watching it. I can't quite figure it out. I don't think anybody can." Clinton, meanwhile, said as little as possible about the situation, preferring to let Giuliani's drama play out on its own;{{cite news | url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9D04E6DB143BF931A25756C0A9669C8B63 | title=Mrs. Clinton Stays Quiet While Mayor Is in Spotlight | author=[[Adam Nagourney]] | newspaper=The New York Times | date=May 12, 2000 | access-date=December 18, 2007}} on May 17, as he huddled with his doctors over whether to choose surgery or radiation as his treatment{{cite news | url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9B05E2DA1F3BF934A25756C0A9669C8B63 | title= Pensively, Giuliani Still Debates His Future | author=[[Elisabeth Bumiller]] | newspaper=The New York Times | date=May 17, 2000 | access-date=December 18, 2007}} while facing conflicting political advice from his aides,{{cite news | url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9B05E2D9103BF936A25756C0A9669C8B63 | title= Conflicting Advice at City Hall Complicates Giuliani's Decision | author=[[Adam Nagourney]] | newspaper=The New York Times | date=May 15, 2000 | access-date=December 18, 2007}} she won the unanimous approval of delegates to the Democratic Party state convention at the [[Pepsi Arena (Albany, New York)|Pepsi Arena]] in [[Albany, New York|Albany]], giving a constrained acceptance speech because she did not know her general election opponent.{{cite news | url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9B03EFD71F3BF934A25756C0A9669C8B63 | title= With Senate Rival Uncertain, Party Nominates Mrs. Clinton | author=[[Adam Nagourney]] | newspaper=The New York Times | date=May 17, 2000 | access-date=December 18, 2007}} Finally, on May 19, Giuliani held what ''The New York Times'' again described as "an emotional, riveting news conference" that "reached a new level of introspection" to announce that he was dropping out of the Senate race:{{cite news | url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9B07E1DF103AF933A15756C0A9669C8B63 | title= The Mayor's Decision: The Overview: Cancer is Concern | author=[[Elisabeth Bumiller]] | newspaper=The New York Times | date=May 20, 2000 | access-date=December 18, 2007}} "This is not the right time for me to run for office. If it were six months ago or it were a year from now or the timing were a little different, maybe it would be different. But it isn't different and that's the way life is." He added that, "I used to think the core of me was in politics, probably. It isn't. When you feel your mortality and your humanity you realize that, that the core of you is first of all being able to take care of your health." He said that he would instead devote the remainder of his mayoralty trying to overcome the hostile relations he had with many of the city's minority groups. === A change of Republicans: Lazio === [[File:Ricklazio.jpg|thumb|146px|right|After Giuliani withdrew in May 2000, lesser-known Long Island congressman Rick Lazio took his place.]] While previous Republican candidates and fellow Long Island congressmen Rick Lazio and Pete King had both indicated an interest in replacing Giuliani,{{cite news | url=http://www.cnn.com/ALLPOLITICS/analysis/rothenberg/2000/05/23/rothenberg/index.html | title=New York Senate race far from settled | author=[[Stuart Rothenberg]] | publisher=[[CNN]] | date=May 23, 2000 | access-date=November 2, 2007}} upon Giuliani's withdrawal the state party quickly rallied around Lazio, who had more campaign funds and who was viewed as a potentially strong candidate. In particular, Governor Pataki — who never cared much for Giuliani to begin with — was strongly in favor of Lazio, and praised him as a "fresh, unencumbered challenger" to Clinton.{{cite news | url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9906E1DF103AF933A15756C0A9669C8B63 | title=Giuliani quits race for Senate, and G.O.P. rallies around Lazio | author=[[Adam Nagourney]] | newspaper=The New York Times | date=May 20, 2000 | access-date=December 18, 2007}} This also caused a shuffle in New York's unique third-party ballot-line alignments: the [[Liberal Party of New York]], which was previously set to run Giuliani (whom they had supported in all three of his mayoral races), now switched to Clinton, while the [[Conservative Party of New York]], which had previously been loath to endorse the socially liberal Giuliani (and was set to nominate former Westchester congressman [[Joe DioGuardi]]) lined up behind Lazio.{{cite news |author=Mahoney, Joe |author2=Goldschlag, William |date=May 23, 2000 |title=GOP Barnstormer Poses With Pataki Upstate |url=https://www.nydailynews.com/2000/05/23/gop-barnstormer-poses-with-pataki-upstate/ |access-date=June 7, 2011 |newspaper=[[Daily News (New York)|Daily News]] |location=New York}} Lazio accepted the unanimous approval of delegates to the Republican Party state convention at a hotel ballroom in [[Buffalo, New York|Buffalo]] on May 30.{{cite news | url=https://www.tribuneindia.com/2000/20000601/world.htm#6 | title=Lazio nominated to face Hillary | agency=[[Associated Press]] | newspaper=The Tribune|location=India | date=May 31, 2000 | access-date=January 17, 2008}} Clinton now faced a lesser-known candidate in Lazio. While a relative moderate among House Republicans,{{cite news | url=http://archives.cnn.com/2000/ALLPOLITICS/stories/05/19/lazio.senate/ | title=Lazio boasts moderate record on some hot-button issues | author=Amy Paulson | publisher=[[CNN]] | date=May 19, 2000 | access-date=December 17, 2007 | url-status=dead | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070920174519/http://archives.cnn.com/2000/ALLPOLITICS/stories/05/19/lazio.senate/ | archive-date=September 20, 2007 }} Lazio had frequently supported former House speaker [[Newt Gingrich]], a largely despised figure among many New Yorkers.{{cite news | url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/tying-rick-to-newt/ | title=Tying Rick To Newt | publisher=[[CBS News]] | date=August 31, 2000 | access-date=December 17, 2007}} Lazio did bring to the table a suburban background familiar to many New Yorkers, and had a reputation as an energetic campaigner.{{cite news | url=https://www.usatoday.com/news/opinion/e1915.htm | title=Lazio nominated to face Clinton | author=Martha T. Moore | newspaper=[[USA Today]] | date=May 30, 2000 | access-date=December 17, 2007}} One formality left were New York's late-in-the-season primary elections on September 12, which in this case merely served to ratify the state party conventions' choices. Lazio won unopposed,{{cite news | url=http://archives.cnn.com/2000/ALLPOLITICS/stories/09/12/primary.day/index.html | title=Hillary Clinton wins New York Democratic primary | publisher=[[CNN]] | date=September 13, 2000 | access-date=January 17, 2008 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20071007062044/http://archives.cnn.com/2000/ALLPOLITICS/stories/09/12/primary.day/index.html |archive-date = October 7, 2007}} while Clinton won 82 percent of the vote{{cite news | url=http://archives.cnn.com/2000/ALLPOLITICS/stories/09/13/primary.day.01/index.html | title=Hillary Clinton, Lazio to debate tonight after winning New York primary races | publisher=[[CNN]] | date=September 13, 2000 | access-date=January 17, 2008 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20060528231005/http://archives.cnn.com/2000/ALLPOLITICS/stories/09/13/primary.day.01/index.html |archive-date = May 28, 2006}} in easily defeating unknown Manhattan doctor Mark McMahon, who ran on the grounds that "the Clintons have tried to hijack the Democratic Party." For her part, Clinton said that she was "surprised, in a way [to see her name in the voting booth]. I stood there for a minute, staring at my name." Lazio (R) |- | align=center|Quinnipiac | align=center|March 23, 1999 | align=center {{party shading/Democratic}}|'''33%''' | align=center|20% |} {{hidden end}} === Campaign === The contest drew considerable national attention and both candidates were well-funded. By the end of the race, Democrat Clinton and Republicans Lazio and Giuliani had spent a combined $90 million,{{cite news | url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9E04E1DB133FF930A25751C1A9669C8B63 | title= Lazio Sets Spending Mark for a Losing Senate Bid | author=Clifford J. Levy | newspaper=The New York Times | date=December 13, 2000 | access-date=February 22, 2008}} the most of any U.S. Senate race in history.As of 2007, it still holds the record of most expensive Senate race. See {{cite news | url=http://www.salon.com/news/feature/2007/11/27/rudy_hillary/ | title=When Rudy Met Hillary | author=Rob Polner | magazine=[[Salon (magazine)|Salon]] | date=November 27, 2007 | access-date=February 22, 2008}} Lazio outspent Clinton $40 million to $29 million, with Clinton also getting several million dollars in [[soft money]] from Democratic organizations. Among Clinton antagonists circles, direct mail-based fundraising groups such as the Emergency Committee to Stop Hillary Rodham Clinton sprung up,{{cite news | url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9C0CE7DE1E31F934A15753C1A9669C8B63 | title= Clinton Rivals Raise Little Besides Rage | author=Clifford J. Levy | newspaper=The New York Times | date=October 27, 2000 | access-date=December 17, 2007}} sending out solicitations regarding the "carpetbagging" issue. Clinton secured a broad base of support, including endorsements from conservation groupsFor example, the [[Sierra Club]] {{cite news | title= Hillary Clinton Is Endorsed By Sierra Club as Better Ally | author=[[Randal C. Archibold]] | url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9C04E3DE1739F935A3575AC0A9669C8B63&n=Top%2fReference%2fTimes%20Topics%2fOrganizations%2fS%2fSierra%20Club | newspaper=The New York Times | date=September 6, 2000 | access-date=October 6, 2007}} and organized labor,{{cite news | title= Hillary Clinton Stars, Unrivaled, at Labor Day Parade | author=Steven Greenhouse | newspaper=The New York Times | date=September 10, 2000 }} but notably not the New York City police union which endorsed Lazio while firefighters supported Clinton.{{cite news | title= Police Union Backs Lazio, Citing First Lady's Statement | url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9902E7DF1339F93BA3575AC0A9669C8B63&n=Top/Reference/Times%20Topics/People/C/Clinton,%20Hillary%20Rodham | author=Elisabeth Bumiller | date=September 8, 2000 | access-date=October 6, 2007 | work=[[The New York Times]]}}{{cite news | title=Clinton wins endorsement of city's firefighter unions | date=April 19, 2006 | access-date=October 6, 2007 | url=http://www.newsday.com/news/nationworld/nation/ny-nyhill0420,0,6369920.story | agency=[[Associated Press]] | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070628055431/http://www.newsday.com/news/nationworld/nation/ny-nyhill0420%2C0%2C6369920.story | archive-date=June 28, 2007 | url-status=dead }} While Clinton had a solid base of support in New York City, candidates and observers expected the race to be decided in upstate New York where 45 percent of the state's voters lived. During the campaign, Clinton vowed to improve the economic picture in upstate New York, promising that her plan would deliver 200,000 New York jobs over six years. Her plan included specific tax credits with the purpose of rewarding job creation and encouraging business investment, especially in the high-tech sector. She called for targeted personal tax cuts for college tuition and long-term care.{{cite news | url=http://archives.cnn.com/2000/ALLPOLITICS/stories/11/07/senate.ny/ | title=Hillary Rodham Clinton scores historic win in New York | publisher=[[CNN]] | date=November 8, 2000 | access-date=December 17, 2007 | url-status=dead | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070212204213/http://archives.cnn.com/2000/ALLPOLITICS/stories/11/07/senate.ny/ | archive-date=February 12, 2007 }} Lazio faced a unique tactical problem campaigning upstate. The major issue there was the persistently weak local economy, which Lazio hoped to link to his opponent's husband's tenure in office. Attacks on the state of the upstate economy were frequently interpreted as criticism of incumbent Republican governor [[George Pataki]], however, limiting the effect of this line of attack. In July 2000, the release of ''State of a Union: Inside the Complex Marriage of Bill and Hillary Clinton'' by author [[Jerry Oppenheimer]] led to reports that Clinton had called someone a "fucking Jew bastard" in 1974.{{cite news | url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2000/jul/18/uselections2000.usa | title=Hillary faces voters' wrath for alleged ethnic slur | first=Michael | last=Ellison | newspaper=[[The Guardian]] | date=July 17, 2000 | access-date=July 31, 2019}} The report, which received international media coverage, "rocked" Clinton's campaign, with ''[[The Daily Telegraph]]'' describing the campaign as having "mounted a frantic damage limitation exercise after details of the alleged incident were leaked".{{cite news | url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/worldnews/northamerica/usa/1349202/Clinton-leaps-to-Hillarys-defence-over-Jewish-slur.html |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20220112/https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/worldnews/northamerica/usa/1349202/Clinton-leaps-to-Hillarys-defence-over-Jewish-slur.html |archive-date=2022-01-12 |url-access=subscription |url-status=live | title=Clinton leaps to Hillary's defence over 'Jewish slur' | first=Toby | last=Harnden | newspaper=[[The Daily Telegraph]] | date=July 18, 2000 | access-date=July 31, 2019}}{{cbignore}} Clinton had reportedly screamed the insult at Paul Fray, who managed Bill Clinton's unsuccessful 1974 congressional campaign. Fray, his wife, and another campaign staffer stated that they had heard Clinton's outburst, while both Clintons adamantly denied that she had referenced Fray's heritage (while Oppenheimer wrote that Fray's father was Jewish,{{cite news | url=https://www.nytimes.com/2000/08/06/books/for-better-or-worse.html | title=For Better or Worse | first=Emily | last=Eakin | work=[[The New York Times Book Review]] | date=August 8, 2000 | page=26 | access-date=September 7, 2019}} in reality Fray was a Southern Baptist whose closest Jewish ancestor was a paternal great-grandmother). Bill Clinton did allow that Hillary might have simply called Fray a "bastard". In media interviews, Fray and his wife acknowledged several factors that tended to undermine his credibility: he had lost his license to practice law for altering court records; he had made false accusations against the Clintons in the past; and he had suffered a brain hemorrhage with some resultant losses of memory.{{cite news | url=https://www.nytimes.com/2000/07/20/nyregion/first-lady-s-aide-asked-help-on-slur-claim.html | title=First Lady's Aide Asked Help on Slur Claim | first=Randal C. | last=Archibold | newspaper=The New York Times | date=July 20, 2000 | page=B4 | access-date=September 7, 2019}} Opponents continued to make the carpetbagging issue a focal point throughout the race and during debates.{{cite news | url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9C0CE4D9103CF93AA35753C1A9669C8B63 | title=Excerpts From Second Debate Between Mrs. Clinton and Lazio | newspaper=The New York Times | date=October 9, 2000 | access-date=February 18, 2008}} [[Talk radio]] hammered on this, with New York-based [[Sean Hannity]] issuing a daily mantra, "Name me three things Hillary Clinton has ever done for the people of New York!" Clinton's supporters pointed out that the state was receptive to national leaders, such as [[Robert F. Kennedy]] who was [[United States Senate election in New York, 1964|elected to the Senate in 1964]] despite similar accusations. In the end, according to exit polls conducted in the race, a majority of the voters dismissed the carpetbagging issue as unimportant.{{Cite web |date=2000-11-08 |title=CARPETBAG TAG DIDN'T TRAVEL Outsider Clinton won 'em over statewide |url=https://www.nydailynews.com/2000/11/08/carpetbag-tag-didnt-travel-outsider-clinton-won-em-over-statewide/ |access-date=2024-09-26 |website=[[New York Daily News]] |language=en-US}} During the campaign, [[Independent Counsel]] [[Robert Ray (prosecutor)|Robert Ray]] filed his final reports regarding the long-running [[Whitewater (controversy)|Whitewater]],[http://archives.cnn.com/2000/ALLPOLITICS/stories/09/20/whitewater/ "Ray: Insufficient evidence to prosecute Clintons in Whitewater probe"] {{webarchive | url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080313092222/http://archives.cnn.com/2000/ALLPOLITICS/stories/09/20/whitewater/ | date=March 13, 2008 }}, [[CNN]], September 20, 2000. Retrieved April 30, 2007. "[[Travelgate]]",[http://archives.cnn.com/2000/ALLPOLITICS/stories/10/18/travel.office "Ray: First lady's answers false in travel office probe, but no prosecution"] {{webarchive | url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080131174436/http://archives.cnn.com/2000/ALLPOLITICS/stories/10/18/travel.office | date=January 31, 2008 }}, [[CNN]], October 18, 2000. Retrieved June 16, 2007. and "[[Filegate]]"Neil A. Lewis, [https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9806EED8173AF934A25750C0A9669C8B63 "Report Clears White House In Inquiry Over F.B.I. Files"], ''The New York Times'', March 17, 2000. Retrieved June 9, 2007. investigations of the White House, each of which included specific investigations of Hillary Clinton actions. The reports exonerated her on the files matter, said there was insufficient evidence regarding her role in Whitewater, and said that she had made factually false statements regarding the Travel Office firings but there was insufficient evidence to prosecute her. Although ''The New York Times'' editorialized that the release of the reports seemed possibly timed to coincide with the Senate election,{{cite news | url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9407EFDA1630F933A0575BC0A9669C8B63 | title= Mr. Ray's Ill-Timed Report | newspaper=The New York Times | date=August 30, 2000 | access-date=February 16, 2008}} in practice the findings were not seen as likely to sway many voters' opinions.{{cite news | url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/whitewater-case-closed/ | title=Whitewater: Case Closed | publisher=[[CBS News]] | date=September 20, 2000 | access-date=February 16, 2008}} A September 13, 2000 debate between Lazio and Clinton proved important. Lazio was on the warpath against [[soft money]] and the amounts of it coming from the [[Democratic National Committee]] into Clinton's campaign, and challenged Clinton to agree to ban soft money from both campaigns. He left his podium and waved his proposed paper agreement in Clinton's face;Gerth, Van Natta Jr., ''Her Way'', pp. 212–213. many debate viewers thought he had invaded her [[personal space]] and as a result Clinton's support among women voters solidified. Late in the campaign, Lazio criticized Clinton for accepting campaign donations from various Arab groups in the wake of the [[USS Cole bombing|USS ''Cole'' bombing]]. The Lazio campaign orchestrated a wave of telephone calls to voters using this attack. This issue caused former New York Mayor [[Ed Koch]] to take out ads telling Lazio to "stop with the sleaze already," and did not change the dynamic of the race. Some of Lazio's campaign strategists would later say that the ''Cole''-based attack had backfired and became the campaign's biggest blunder. === Results === A lawyer following the matter stated that even if Clinton had promised to lobby her husband for clemency in exchange for the town's votes — a claim for which there was no proof — it would be difficult to establish a crime had taken place: "Politicians make promises all the time. That's nothing new — or illegal." Clinton acknowledged sitting in on a post-election meeting discussing possible clemency for the four, but said she had played no part in her husband's decision. A federal investigation launched to investigate various Clinton pardons, closed its investigation of the New Square matter in June 2002 by taking no action against Bill, Hillary Clinton, or any residents of New Square.{{cite news | url=http://archives.cnn.com/2002/ALLPOLITICS/06/20/clinton.clemency/index.html | title=Clinton cleared in one probe of clemency grants | publisher=[[CNN]] | date=June 20, 2002 | access-date=May 24, 2007 | url-status=dead | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071106043804/http://archives.cnn.com/2002/ALLPOLITICS/06/20/clinton.clemency/index.html | archive-date=November 6, 2007 }} === Hollywood fundraiser === [[file:Hillary Clinton and her largest donor Peter Paul.jpg|thumb|146px|right|Hillary Clinton with her largest 2000 contributor, Peter Paul, at the [[Gala Hollywood Farewell Salute to President Clinton]].]] Hillary Clinton's former finance director, [[David Rosen (politics)|David Rosen]], was indicted on January 7, 2005, on campaign finance charges related to a fundraising event produced by [[Peter F. Paul]]. Paul, a convicted drug dealer who would soon after be convicted on stock fraud charges after being extradited from Brazil, stated that he spent $1.2 million to produce the August 12, 2000 [[Hollywood Gala Salute to President William Jefferson Clinton]] event, which was both a tribute to honor President Clinton and a fundraiser for the First Lady's 2000 Senate campaign. The [[United States Department of Justice|Justice Department]] indictment charged Rosen with filing false reports with the [[Federal Election Commission]] by reporting only $400,000 in contributions. On May 27, 2005, the jury acquitted Rosen on all counts.{{cite news | url=https://news.yahoo.com/s/ap/20050527/ap_on_re_us/clinton_fundraising_probe | title=~ Clinton Fundraising Probe | agency=[[Associated Press]] | publisher= [[Yahoo! News]] | date=May 27, 2005}} On January 5, 2006, it was reported that Clinton's campaign group agreed to pay a $35,000 fine related to the underreporting of the fundraiser's expenses.{{cite news | url=http://www.cnn.com/2006/POLITICS/01/05/hillaryclinton.fundra.ap/index.html | title=~ Hillary Clinton Fundraising | publisher=[[CNN]] | date=January 5, 2006 | url-status=dead | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060111134000/http://www.cnn.com/2006/POLITICS/01/05/hillaryclinton.fundra.ap/index.html | archive-date=January 11, 2006 }} Peter Paul also filed a civil suit in this matter, ''[[Paul v. Clinton]]''. On April 10, 2006, the judge in charge of the case removed Hillary Clinton as a defendant, citing a lack of evidence, but leaving open the possibility that she might still be called to testify as a witness in the case.{{cite news | url=http://www.nysun.com/article/30698?access=709915 | title=Judge Drops Senator Clinton From Lawsuit | author=Josh Gerstein | newspaper=[[The New York Sun]] | date=April 10, 2006 | access-date=December 17, 2007}} The removal was upheld by the [[California Courts of Appeal#Second District|California Second District Court of Appeal]] on October 16, 2007.{{cite news | url=http://www.wtop.com/?nid=213&sid=1270070 | title=Court Says Clinton Should Not Be in Suit | author=Greg Risling | agency=[[Associated Press]] | publisher= [[WTOP-FM|WTOP]] | date=October 16, 2007 | access-date=November 1, 2007}} Meanwhile, by the time of [[Hillary Rodham Clinton presidential campaign, 2008|Hillary Clinton's 2008 presidential campaign]], a 13-minute video produced by Paul and describing his various allegations against Hillary Clinton had become quite popular on the Internet, gaining 1.4 million hits on [[Google Video]] and about 350,000 on [[YouTube]] in a single week in October 2007.{{cite news | url=http://www.sddt.com/News/article.cfm?SourceCode=20071030ft#.UJZh_YYpC_Q | title=Anti-Hillary Clinton video finding a niche on the Internet | author=Jim Kuhnhenn | agency=[[Associated Press]] | date=October 30, 2007 | access-date=November 4, 2012 | newspaper=[[San Diego Daily Transcript]]}} === Analysis === Clinton won the election on November 7 with 55 percent of the vote to Lazio's 43 percent,{{cite web | url=http://www.fec.gov/pubrec/fe2000/2000senate.htm#NY | title=Federal Elections 2000: U.S. Senate results | publisher=[[Federal Election Commission]] | access-date=December 17, 2007}} a difference larger than most observers had expected.{{cite news | url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9C06E7D71638F93AA35752C1A9669C8B63 | title=First Lady Emerges From Shadow And Begins to Cast Her Own | author=[[Elisabeth Bumiller]], Dean E. Murphy | newspaper=[[The New York Times]] | date=November 9, 2000 | access-date=February 16, 2008}} Clinton won the traditionally Democratic base of New York City by large margins, and carried suburban [[Westchester County, New York|Westchester County]], but lost heavily populated [[Long Island]], part of which Lazio represented in Congress. She won 13 of 61 counties, with surprising victories in Upstate counties, such as [[Cayuga County, New York|Cayuga]], [[Rensselaer County, New York|Rensselaer]], and [[Niagara County, New York|Niagara]]. Overall, she lost Upstate to Lazio by only 3 percentage points, to which her win has been attributed. In comparison with other results, Clinton's 12-point margin was smaller than Gore's 25-point margin over Bush in the [[United States presidential election in New York, 2000|concurrent presidential contest within the state]]; was slightly larger than the 10-point margin by which fellow New York senator [[Chuck Schumer]] defeated incumbent Republican [[Al D'Amato]] in the hotly contested [[1998 United States Senate election in New York|1998 senate race]]; and was considerably smaller than the 47-point margin by which Senator Schumer won reelection in [[2004 United States Senate election in New York|2004 senate race]] against little-known Republican challenger [[Howard Mills]].{{cite news | url=http://www.cnn.com/ELECTION/1998/states/NY/S/index.html | title=Election Night 1998: New York | publisher=[[CNN]] | date=November 4, 1998 | access-date=December 17, 2007}}{{cite news | url=https://www.usatoday.com/news/politicselections/vote2004/ny.htm | title=Kerry, Schumer win in New York | agency=[[Associated Press]] | newspaper=[[USA Today]] | date=November 3, 2004 | access-date=December 17, 2007}} The victory of a Democrat in the Senate election was not assured, because in recent decades the Republicans had won about half the elections for governor and senator. Lazio's bid was handicapped by the weak performance of [[George W. Bush]] in New York in the 2000 election,{{cite news | url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9E0DE2DF1738F93AA35752C1A9669C8B63 | title=Mrs. Clinton Found Right Mix in Fame and Upstate Focus | author=[[Adam Nagourney]] | newspaper=[[The New York Times]]| date=November 9, 2000 | access-date=February 18, 2008}} but it was also clear Hillary Clinton had made substantial inroads in upstate New York prior to Lazio's entry into the race. Exit polls also showed a large gender gap with Clinton running stronger than expected among moderate women and unaffiliated women.{{cite news | url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9F01E1DF1238F931A25752C1A9669C8B63 | title=It Took a Woman; How Gender Helped Elect Hillary Clinton | author=[[Elisabeth Bumiller]] | newspaper=[[The New York Times]] | date=November 12, 2000 | access-date=January 15, 2008}} Clinton's victory would establish her as an effective campaigner and an electoral force on her own, able to capture Republican and independent votes and overcome her polarizing image. She would [[United States Senate election in New York, 2006|easily win re-election in 2006]], and in 2007 began [[Hillary Rodham Clinton presidential campaign, 2008|her presidential campaign for 2008]]. Lazio gave up his House seat to run for Senate. Following his defeat, which set a record for the most money spent in a losing Senate effort, he took positions in the corporate world and avoided electoral politics until becoming a candidate in [[New York gubernatorial election, 2010|New York's 2010 gubernatorial election]].{{Cite news |last=Rutkoff |first=Aaron |date=2 June 2010 |title=GOP Backs Lazio in Race for Governor |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/BL-METROB-3632 |access-date=26 September 2024 |work=[[The Wall Street Journal]]}} However, he was defeated by a wide margin in the Republican primary.{{cite news | url=https://www.nytimes.com/2010/09/28/nyregion/28lazio.html | title=Lazio Leaves Race, Giving Reluctant Aid to a Rival | author=Halbfinger, David M. | newspaper=[[The New York Times]] | date=September 27, 2010 | access-date=September 28, 2010}} Giuliani would undergo treatment for his cancer and eventually recover; he would also divorce Donna Hanover and eventually marry Judith Nathan. After his campaign withdrawal, his political future looked uncertain at best. But less than a year after the Senate general election, the [[September 11 attacks]] took place, with Giuliani still mayor. Giuliani's performance in the aftermath of September 11 earned him many accolades and resurrected his political prospects.{{cite news | url=http://archive.boston.com/news/nation/articles/2007/11/08/skills_at_ready_when_crisis_struck/ | author=Mooney, Brian C. | title=Skills at ready when crisis struck | newspaper=[[The Boston Globe]] | date=November 8, 2007 | access-date=February 18, 2008}} After a successful stint in the private sector, in 2007 he also began [[Rudy Giuliani presidential campaign, 2008|his presidential campaign for 2008]]. Throughout much of 2007, Clinton and Giuliani led in national polls for their parties' respective nominations, and media reports often looked back to the 2000 "race that wasn't" as a preview of what might lie in wait for the entire nation in 2008. Such extrapolating ended with the Giuliani campaign's precipitous decline and January 2008 withdrawal. Clinton as well failed to gain the 2008 nomination and, in June 2008, she finished in a close second place to Illinois senator [[Barack Obama]]. In December 2008, Lowey would have another chance at the Senate seat, when Clinton was nominated for [[U.S. Secretary of State]] by President-elect Obama and Lowey was considered a front-runner to be named as her appointed replacement.{{cite news | url=https://www.politico.com/blogs/politico-now/2008/12/lowey-withdraws-from-race-to-replace-clinton-014481 | title=Lowey withdraws from race to replace Clinton | author=Thrush, Glenn | newspaper=[[Politico]] | date=December 1, 2008 | access-date=December 5, 2008}} But Lowey withdrew from consideration, as in the intervening years she had gained enough seniority to become one of the powerful "cardinals" on the [[United States House Committee on Appropriations|House Appropriations Committee]] and did not want to relinquish that position. When [[Caroline Kennedy]] announced her interest in the vacancy, comparisons were drawn to Clinton in 2000, with both being famous people seeking to hold elective office for the first time.{{cite news | url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2008/dec/18/caroline-kennedy-senate-profile | title=Caroline Kennedy: Born survivor makes Senate bid | author=Goldenberg, Suzanne | newspaper=[[The Guardian]] | date=December 18, 2008 | access-date=March 21, 2009 | location=London}} Others pointed out that Clinton had won election to the office while Kennedy would first be appointed.{{cite news | url=http://www.salon.com/politics/war_room/2008/12/16/kennedy_clinton/ | title=Why Caroline Kennedy is not Hillary Clinton | author=Koppelman, Alex | magazine=[[Salon (magazine)|Salon]] | date=December 16, 2008 | access-date=March 21, 2009}} In any case, Kennedy's effort soon faltered, in part due to not having the same desire or willingness to work for the seat as Clinton had had,{{cite news | url=http://cityroom.blogs.nytimes.com/2008/12/31/choice-of-kennedy-for-senate-no-longer-seems-inevitable | title=Choice of Kennedy for Senate No Longer Seems Inevitable | author=Lee, Jennifer 8. | newspaper=[[The New York Times]] | date=December 31, 2008 | access-date=March 21, 2009}} and she soon withdrew as abruptly as she had entered.{{cite news | url=http://cityroom.blogs.nytimes.com/2008/12/31/choice-of-kennedy-for-senate-no-longer-seems-inevitable | title=Caroline Kennedy officially withdraws from race for Secretary of State Hillary Clinton's Senate seat | author=Lovett, Kenneth | newspaper=[[Daily News (New York)|Daily News]]|location=New York | date=January 22, 2009 | access-date=March 21, 2009}} [[Kirsten Gillibrand]] received the appointment, and attention then turned to who would run against her in the [[United States Senate special election in New York, 2010|2010 Senate special election]]. By November 2009, Giuliani was seriously considering a run for his old would-have-been Senate seat,{{cite news | url=http://www.nydailynews.com/news/politics/2009/11/19/2009-11-19_former_mayor_rudy_giuliani_to_announce_plan_to_run_for_us_senate.html | title=Rudy Giuliani will very likely seek U.S. Senate seat, and if elected maybe 2012 White House: source | author=Kenneth Lovett | author2=Elizabeth Benjamin | author3=David Saltonstall | newspaper=[[Daily News (New York)|Daily News]]|location=New York | date=November 19, 2009 | access-date=February 21, 2010}} but the following month he announced he was not running for it or anything else in 2010, signalling an end to his political career.{{cite news | url=https://www.nytimes.com/2009/12/23/nyregion/23rudy.html | title=Giuliani Says Farewell, for Now, to Politics | author=Michael Powell | newspaper=[[The New York Times]] | date=December 22, 2009 |
